title: The next chapter for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
text: Building and operating a data warehouse is increasingly a software engineering discipline. Teams want to develop warehouse changes in isolation, version them in Git, review them through pull requests, promote them safely across environments, and automate the entire process using their existing CI/CD systems. Over the past several releases, we've been evolving CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse around that lifecycle: DacFx established a common schema deployment foundation. Pre, and post-deployment scripts expanded deployments beyond schema changes. Warehouse Item Definition APIs opened the same lifecycle to automation. Together, these investments are creating a more complete CI/CD lifecycle for Fabric Warehouse, from developing and versioning database changes to deploying and automating them across environments. Let’s take a closer look at how each capability moves that experience forward, what’s available today, and what we’re building next. What we've delivered Establishing a consistent deployment foundation with DacFx The first challenge was making Warehouse deployments behave like database deployments, not artifact copies. A Warehouse contains state, data, dependencies, and relationships between database objects. Moving a change from development to production therefore requires understanding what changed and how those changes should be applied to the target database . This is where DacFx became foundational to the experience. With Git Integration , it is represented as a SQL database project in source control. Developers can work using familiar Git practices such as branching, commits, and pull requests. When those changes are synchronized back to Fabric, DacFx understands the database model and determines the schema changes that need to be applied. Figure: Git-based development workflow in Microsoft Fabric , enabling isolated feature development, collaboration through pull requests, and synchronization of Fabric items across feature and shared workspaces, with infrastructure managed as code. We extended that same foundation to deployment pipelines . When a Warehouse moves between development, test and production environments, DacFx compares source and target states and generates the incremental deployment required to move the target to the desired state. Figure: End-to-end CI/CD workflow in Microsoft Fabric , combining Git-based feature development with deployment pipelines to promote Fabric items consistently across development, test, and production environments. That established a consistent path: Develop → Version in Git → Review → Deploy → Validate → Promote. Pre, and post-deployment scripts A production deployment rarely consists of schema changes alone. Teams often need to prepare data before a deployment, seed or initialize data afterward, or execute SQL actions that need to happen at a specific point in the release. To support that workflow, we introduced pre, and post-deployment scripts . A shared SQL query can be designated as a pre, or post-deployment script and becomes part of the SQL project. The designation travels with the Warehouse through Git, allowing those actions to be versioned and deployed together with the database definition. The resulting deployment lifecycle becomes pre-deployment actions → DacFx schema deployment → post-deployment actions Figure: Pre, and post-deployment script configuration in Fabric Warehouse , enabling developers to define SQL scripts that execute automatically before and after schema deployment as part of the CI/CD lifecycle. This moves more of the database release process into the CI/CD definition rather than leaving teams to coordinate separate manual steps. Learn more about pre and post-deployment scripts . Warehouse Item Definition APIs Git integration and deployment pipelines provide built-in Fabric experiences, but enterprise CI/CD also needs to work outside the Fabric portal. Customers have existing build systems, automation frameworks and release pipelines and need a programmatic way to manage Warehouse definitions. Warehouse Item Definition APIs are the next part of that foundation. Warehouse definitions support SQL project and DACPAC formats , and Fabric APIs can be used to create a Warehouse from a definition, retrieve its current definition, or update it programmatically. Learn more about the Warehouse REST APIs . This means the same Warehouse definition that underpins Git integration can also participate in API-driven CI/CD workflows. Bringing Familiar Warehouse Development Experiences to Client Tools A complete CI/CD experience starts well before deployment. Developers need familiar tools to build, compare, validate, and manage database changes throughout the development lifecycle. Alongside our DacFx investments, we've strengthened Fabric Warehouse support across SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and Visual Studio Code , bringing familiar SQL development workflows closer to the Fabric web experience. These investments include: Database project support in SSMS: Develop and manage Warehouse schemas using SQL database projects and familiar database development workflows. Schema Compare in VS Code: Compare database schemas, review differences, and generate the changes needed to synchronize environments. Consistent database development: Use the same SQL project and DacFx foundation whether developing in the Fabric portal or client tools. Pre, and post-deployment scripts: Maintain deployment scripts as part of the database project, enabling a consistent deployment experience across web-based and client-based development workflows. The goal is simple: developers should be able to choose their preferred development environment without changing how their database projects are versioned, built, or deployed. This brings together the flexibility of familiar SQL development tools with the integrated CI/CD experience in Fabric Warehouse. What's next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse Building on this foundation, we’re focusing on three investments: Deployment configurations: Give developers control over how changes are applied. Cover data handling, object handling, and error handling. Apply different behaviors per environment, such as permissive in development and stricter in production. Fabric CI/CD package (fabric-cicd) support for Warehouse: Simplify end-to-end automation. Deploy Warehouse definitions from source control alongside other Fabric items. Integrate with systems like Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions. CI/CD for SQL analytics endpoint: Extend Git integration and deployment pipelines using the same SQL project and DacFx foundation. Lay the groundwork for coordinated deployments across dependent Fabric items in medallion and data mesh architectures. The goal: Move from CI/CD for individual items to a consistent, predictable, automated lifecycle for interconnected Fabric analytics solutions. Get started with CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse Connect your Warehouse to Git: Set up Git integration to version your Warehouse as a SQL database project and develop changes in isolation. Promote changes across environments: Use deployment pipelines to move Warehouse changes from development to test and production. Automate data actions around your releases: Configure pre and post-deployment scripts so data preparation and seeding travel with your database definition. Integrate with your existing CI/CD systems: Use the Warehouse REST APIs to create, retrieve, and update Warehouse definitions programmatically. Try these capabilities today and share your feedback in Fabric Ideas | Microsoft Fabric Community . Your input directly shapes what we build next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse.

title: Use OneLake as native storage for Azure Databricks (Preview)
text: Organizations increasingly use Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks together so teams can choose the tools that best fit their data engineering, analytics, and AI workloads while working from a common data foundation. OneLake external-location support for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog is now generally available in Microsoft Fabric, with OneLake Security enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. On the Azure Databricks side, the feature is in preview. With this integration, supported Unity Catalog-managed data can be stored directly in OneLake. To understand the setup and supported scenarios, Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location . Why this matters Data teams often need Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric in the same architecture. Without a shared storage approach, organizations may create copies of the same data for different platforms, introduce pipelines whose primary purpose is synchronization, and manage access independently across multiple storage locations. Using OneLake as managed storage for supported Unity Catalog objects gives organizations a common physical data foundation while preserving flexibility in the services used above it. Azure Databricks continues to provide compute and Unity Catalog management, while OneLake provides the storage destination and Fabric-side data-access controls. What's new in this release This release builds on the Beta announcement , which introduced OneLake external-location support for Unity Catalog. OneLake Security is now enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items, so no user gets access when the item is created. Fabric workspace roles, including Admin, Member, and Contributor, cannot grant access to the data stored in Azure Databricks Storage item and managed through Unity Catalog. Only the Azure Databricks identity can read and write to Azure Databricks Storage items. The updated security experience helps platform teams move from testing connectivity to planning controlled adoption. One shared data foundation, with flexibility above it Use OneLake as the storage foundation Azure Databricks workloads can create supported Unity Catalog-managed data directly in OneLake. A Unity Catalog external location points to an Azure Databricks Storage item in OneLake, and a catalog or schema can use that external location as managed storage. Continue using Unity Catalog-managed objects Teams can continue using Azure Databricks and Unity Catalog to create and manage supported managed tables, volumes, views, materialized views, and streaming tables. The objects remain managed through the Azure Databricks experience while their underlying supported data is stored in OneLake. Keep platform responsibilities clear Azure Databricks remains the environment for Databricks compute and Unity Catalog management. Microsoft Fabric provides the capacity-backed workspace and Azure Databricks Storage item, while OneLake provides the physical storage foundation. How it works Provision storage in Microsoft Fabric: Create a capacity-backed Fabric workspace and an Azure Databricks Storage item. The storage item provides the OneLake location used by the integration. Configure the Azure Databricks identity: Use the managed identity of an Access Connector for Azure Databricks, or a service principal. Assign it the Viewer role on the Fabric workspace, then add it as the only member of a ReadWrite OneLake security role on the Azure Databricks Storage item. Create the Unity Catalog connection: In Azure Databricks, create a storage credential for the approved identity, and then create a OneLake external location that points to the Azure Databricks Storage item. Create Unity Catalog objects: Configure a catalog or schema to use the OneLake external location as managed storage. Data written by supported Azure Databricks workloads is then stored directly in OneLake. Security OneLake security is enabled by default for the Azure Databricks storage item, so no user gets access when the item is created. Fabric workspace roles (Administrator, Member, Contributor, and Viewer) cannot grant access to the data in Azure Databricks storage item. To keep your data secure and under Unity Catalog governance: Add only the Azure Databricks access connector's managed identity to the OneLake security role. Do not add any other users, groups or service principals. Fabric users should read data through mirrored items, not through the storage directly. Only the Azure Databricks identity should access the storage item: Unity Catalog is the single place where you grant, review, and revoke access to the data. How to read the data in Fabric Fabric users read the data through a mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item, not through the Azure Databricks Storage item. The mirrored catalog item shows the Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, and tables you select in a Fabric workspace, without copying the data. Analysts and engineers can query it through the SQL analytics endpoint, notebooks, and Power BI reports. You can create the mirrored catalog item from either platform: From Azure Databricks, with Publish to Fabric : Run it on the catalog you want to share, and it creates the mirrored catalog item in the Fabric workspace you choose. This route suits data engineers who already work in Azure Databricks. From Microsoft Fabric, as a new Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item: Connect to your Azure Databricks workspace, then choose the catalog, schemas, or tables to include. This route suits Fabric administrators and analysts who manage the workspace. Fabric readers use the mirrored catalog item. Never add them to the storage item's OneLake security role, which is reserved for the Azure Databricks identity. Get started Ready to use OneLake as managed storage for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog objects? Start with the Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location tutorial and plan your deployment.

title: Securing and governing your medallion layers in Fabric Data Warehouse
text: Coauthor - Artur Vieira Part 4 of a series on medallion architecture with Fabric Data Warehouse. Security should follow the layers, not fight them. In Part 1 we chose the pattern, in Part 2 we built the layers, and in Part 3 we covered the operating practices that keep them healthy. Security is the natural next step, because a medallion architecture already gives you something most platforms do not: three clearly different audiences. A medallion architecture creates clear boundaries between raw, refined, and curated data. Applying security and governance at those boundaries helps reduce unnecessary exposure, simplify access decisions, and give each audience the data it needs without opening every layer.. The following approach shows how to secure and govern a medallion pipeline in Fabric Data Warehouse. Why this matters Most access problems in analytics platforms are not dramatic breaches. They are cases of unnecessary access, such as an analyst who can read raw customer records because the entire warehouse was shared or a service account with more permissions than its task requires. A medallion architecture simplifies this work because each layer already signals a different level of sensitivity. Raw data is typically the most exposed and least useful to a business user, while curated data is shaped for broader consumption. The security model should follow that progression. The goal is simple: as data moves toward Gold, the audience can expand because the data has been cleaned, shaped, and protected for broader use. Rule 1: Separate the layers before you secure them Access control is much easier when the layers are separate objects. This is the same layout rule from Part 1, now with a security payoff. In Fabric, if Bronze, Silver, and Gold live in separate workspaces, you can keep the Bronze workspace restricted to a small engineering group while giving a wider audience access to the Gold workspace. Separate workspaces also provide clearer access boundaries and can help isolate workloads across the medallion layers. Workspace roles and item permissions are not the same thing, and the difference matters for medallion. Admin, Member, and Contributor all receive CONTROL on every warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint in the workspace: full read/write access plus the ability to manage SQL permissions. Viewer receives CONNECT and ReadData, so viewers can read every table and view with T-SQL. When you share a single warehouse instead, you choose the level: Read lets the recipient connect only, “Read all data using SQL” grants ReadData (the equivalent of db_datareader), and “Read all data using Apache Spark” grants ReadAll over the warehouse’s files in OneLake. ReadData and ReadAll are separate permissions that do not overlap. Treat ReadAll as an engineering permission: row-level and column-level security apply only to queries on the warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint, so Spark access to the underlying files should go only to people who are allowed to see everything in that layer. Access path What it grants Typical use in a medallion design Workspace Admin, Member, Contributor CONTROL on every warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint; sees unmasked data Engineers who build and operate the layer Workspace Viewer CONNECT and ReadData on every warehouse in the workspace Read-only consumers of a whole workspace, usually Gold Item share: Read Connect only; no table access until granted with T-SQL Granular, object-by-object access Item share: Read all data using SQL (ReadData) Read-only access to all tables and views, like db_datareader Gold consumers and report users Item share: Read all data using Apache Spark (ReadAll) Access to the warehouse’s files in OneLake through Spark Engineers who need Spark; grant sparingly Do this well: Put each layer in its own workspace when governance matters, or at least in its own Fabric item. Assign workspace roles deliberately. Admin, Member, Contributor, and Viewer are not interchangeable. Give analysts Viewer access to Gold and no path into the Bronze workspace at all. Share Gold with “Read all data using SQL” for consumers, or share with Read only and add T-SQL GRANTs when they should see just some objects. Rule of thumb: if one workspace role grants access to raw and curated data at the same time, the layout is doing security a disservice. Rule 2: Grant the least privilege each layer needs Within a warehouse, Fabric Data Warehouse supports granular SQL permissions. You can grant or deny access to schemas, tables, views, and procedures, which is especially useful when multiple medallion layers share one warehouse. If Bronze and Silver sit in the same warehouse separated by schemas, revoke general read access on the Bronze schema and let only engineers or a service identity use it. Most consumers should never need more than read access to Gold. Do this well: Default to read-only for anyone who consumes data rather than builds it. Give pipelines and service identities only the permissions their job requires, on the layers they actually touch. Review permissions when a layer changes owners, not only when someone complains about access. Rule of thumb: many people need Gold, a few need Silver, and very few should need Bronze. Rule 3: Use row-level security when one table serves many audiences Row-level security in Fabric Data Warehouse controls which rows a user can view based on group membership or execution context. This lets one Gold table safely support audiences such as different regions, departments, or customers without creating a separate table for each group. This belongs mostly in Gold. That is where a single fact table often serves several regions, departments, or customers at once. Bronze and Silver are usually restricted to a small team already, so filtering rows there solves a problem you should not have. One scope note: row-level and column-level security apply to queries on the warehouse or SQL analytics endpoint. Power BI semantic models in Direct Lake mode fall back to DirectQuery to honor them, so include that in your Gold performance testing. Do this well: Apply row-level security to every table that requires audience-specific filtering. If a table has no row-level security policy, users with access to that table can view all rows permitted by their other assigned permissions. Account for pipeline identities in the predicate, so data movement is not blocked by the filter. Test as a restricted user, not only as an administrator, so modeling mistakes surface before publication. Rule of thumb: use row-level security to share one trusted table safely, not to compensate for a missing Gold model. Rule 4: Protect sensitive columns instead of hoping nobody queries them Some fields should not travel all the way to Gold. The cleanest control is simply not exposing a sensitive column in the curated layer at all. When a sensitive field must remain in the warehouse, use column-level security to block access for roles that should not see it. Use dynamic data masking when the column must remain available but its value should be obscured for users without permission to view the original data. Implement column-level security with a GRANT SELECT that lists only the permitted columns; any query that touches another column fails. Masking behaves differently. Administrators, members, and contributors hold CONTROL on the warehouse and see unmasked data by default, and a user with query access can infer masked values through range filters. Use masking to prevent accidental exposure, and rely on column-level security and least privilege when a value must stay hidden. Do this well: Drop identifiers in Silver or Gold when the business question does not need them. Use column-level security when a role should not see a field at all, and masking when the field must be present but obscured. Grant the unmask narrowly and treat it as a decision worth recording. title: Announcing the retirement of R and Python visuals in Power BI
text: The built-in R and Python visuals in Power BI will retire in May 2027 . What changes This retirement applies only to R and Python visuals in interactive Power BI reports. Python scripts used in Power Query to populate tables are not affected. Power BI service: At retirement, all R and Python visuals will stop working in published reports, including those published before retirement. R-powered custom visuals: Custom visuals that use R will also no longer work at retirement. Older versions of Power BI Desktop: These visuals will continue to work locally using R and Python installed on your machine. Future versions of Power BI Desktop: After retirement, R and Python visuals will be removed, so you won't be able to add them to reports. What you need to do No migration within your report will recreate your exact R or Python visual. You must replace it with a different visualization before retirement. Start reviewing your reports for R and Python visuals and communicate within your organization that reports using them will be impacted. Preserve their scripts and dependencies. If you use Power BI project (PBIP) format and Git-integrated workspaces , search your report definitions in source control to find these visuals across multiple reports. Look for the visualType values pythonVisual for Python visuals and scriptVisual for R visuals. Keep the visualization in your report. Rebuild it with a built-in Power BI visual or an existing custom visual . AI coding tools can also help you create a visual with the Power BI custom visuals software development kit (SDK) . The Power BI roadmap includes planned HTML and Vega core visuals for more flexible report visualizations. Check the roadmap for planned availability. Recreate the analysis or visualization outside the report. Explore these alternatives: Fabric notebooks : Recreate the analysis and visualization in a notebook. Scripts may need changes for supported languages, libraries, and data access. Fabric Apps : Explore this option for visualizations that can't be recreated in a Power BI report. Both Fabric notebooks and Fabric Apps can be added to Organizational Apps to share them with your audience. Next steps Test your replacement and let report consumers know what's changing before retirement. If you view an affected report but don't own it, contact the report owner. Learn more in the R visuals documentation and Python visuals documentation . Share feedback on this retirement in the comments.

title: Unifying SQL Pools: Upcoming changes to UI and APIs
text: SQL pools are Fabric Data Warehouse’s built-in workload management capability. They help administrators organize workloads and control how compute resources are allocated across them. SQL pool configurations are represented differently depending on whether a workspace uses the built-in or custom pool model. With unified SQL pools, we’re removing that distinction and representing all pools through a single configuration model across the UI and APIs. This removes the need to switch between built-in and custom modes, making SQL pool configurations easier to understand and manage consistently across the UI and APIs. What's changing and when This blog provides advance notice of upcoming changes to SQL pool configuration management in Fabric Data Warehouse. We're introducing a unified configuration model that removes the distinction between built-in and custom SQL pools. By mid-December 2026: Customers should stop relying on customSQLPoolsEnabled flag to retrieve previously submitted inactive pool configurations. With unification, GET APIs will return only effective configurations, and inactive configurations will no longer be surfaced in the UI or APIs. Beginning January 2027 : New workspaces will use a unified default configuration with a single read-optimized SQL pool that has access to 100% of available compute resources to serve all workloads. Existing workspaces will retain their active configurations and workload behavior. Updated documentation will be published alongside the January rollout. What this means for customers Unified SQL pools simplify the configuration experience without requiring existing customers to migrate or reconfigure their SQL pools. Scenario What customers can expect Existing workspaces Active SQL pool configurations and workload behavior remain unchanged. However, previously submitted inactive configurations will no longer be surfaced in the UI or GET API responses. New workspaces New workspaces use the unified SQL pool model by default, with 'Optimize for Reads’ enabled. The configuration can be customized based on workload requirements. Customers with ingestion-heavy workloads and limited cache-reuse needs should review this setting. API integrations The customSQLPoolsEnabled flag will be removed as part of unification. Applications relying on this flag will need to update their logic to use the pool configuration directly. Performance and cost considerations for new workspaces The following performance and cost implications apply only to new workspaces. Existing workspaces will retain their current SQL pool configurations and workload behavior. With unified SQL pools, new workspaces will allow SELECT and non-SELECT workloads to access up to 100% of available compute resources, compared to the current default allocation of 50% for each workload type. SELECT workloads: Queries can access up to 100% of available compute instead of 50%, potentially improving performance but also increasing compute consumption. Non-SELECT workloads: Operations such as data ingestion can also access up to 100% of available compute , potentially completing faster but consuming more compute. Actual performance and cost impact will depend on workload patterns and resource utilization. To manage consumption, customers can: Allocate smaller resource percentages to individual pools to limit their maximum potential compute consumption. Disabling Optimize for Reads: For ingestion-heavy workloads with limited cache reuse, consider turning off Optimize for Reads to avoid unnecessary cache-related consumption. Reducing cache cooldown: Once configurable cache cooldown becomes available , shorten the default five-minute cooldown (for example, to one minute) through the UI or API to reduce the time compute remains allocated after activity. What API consumers should update If you integrate with SQL Pools REST APIs , review your client logic before the unified SQL pools rollout: By mid-December 2026: Stop relying on customSQLPoolsEnabled flag to retrieve previously submitted inactive configurations. Update your clients to read and render only the effective configuration returned by GET. Before the January 2027 rollout: Remove logic that branches on built-in versus custom mode, and prepare for the removal of customSQLPoolsEnabled from PATCH requests. Changes to GET API responses With unified SQL pools, GET responses will reflect only the configuration currently in effect for the workspace. Previously submitted custom pool configurations with customSQLPoolsEnabled was false that are not active, will no longer be returned by the API or displayed in the UI. Scenario Current behavior After unification customSQLPoolsEnabled = true GET returns the custom pool configuration. GET returns the effective pool configuration. customSQLPoolsEnabled = false, but custom configurations were previously submitted GET may return those inactive custom configurations. GET returns only the effective configuration. Inactive custom configurations are not resurfaced. Existing workspace with active custom pools Active configuration is returned. Active configuration remains unchanged and is returned. Changes to PATCH API Now, the PATCH API uses the customSQLPoolsEnabled flag to distinguish between built-in and custom SQL pool configurations. With unification, this flag will be removed from the PATCH request, and clients will manage SQL pools directly through the configuration payload. The examples below illustrate this change. The only difference is the removal of customSQLPoolsEnabled ; the SQL pool configuration payload remains the same. Before unification (current behavior): PATCH https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/workspaces/ /warehouses/sqlPoolsConfiguration { "customSQLPoolsEnabled": true, "customSQLPools": [ { "name": "ETL", "isDefault": false, "maxResourcePercentage": 20, "optimizeForReads": false, "classifier": { "type": "Application Name", "value": [ "ETL", "Load", "Pipeline" ] } } ] } After unification (proposed behavior): PATCH https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/workspaces/ /warehouses/sqlPoolsConfiguration { "customSQLPools": [ { "name": "ETL", "isDefault": false, "maxResourcePercentage": 20, "optimizeForReads": false, "classifier": { "type": "Application Name", "value": [ "ETL", "Load", "Pipeline" ] } } ] } Next steps Existing workspace configurations will remain unchanged, but API consumers should review dependencies on customSQLPoolsEnabled flag and prepare for the unified model. For new workspaces, consider customizing pool allocations and 'Optimize for Reads ' settings based on performance and cost requirements. Refer to the SQL Pools REST API documentation for the current API behavior. Updated documentation will be published alongside the rollout.

title: A Leader in Data Integration—six years running
text: Microsoft is a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Data Integration Tools For the sixth consecutive year, Microsoft has been named a Leader in the 2026 Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Data Integration Tools—and this year, the story isn't just about unifying data, it's about what customers are building on it. In our view, it reflects how far Microsoft Fabric has come—from a unified platform to an open, AI-ready foundation that connects data across clouds, formats, and partners. Gartner evaluates vendors on two critical dimensions: Completeness of Vision and Ability to Execute. Microsoft offers Microsoft Fabric, Azure Data Factory, SQL Server Data Integration Services (SSIS), Power Query, and Azure Synapse Analytics as its data integration tools. The report noted Microsoft’s global reach, industry diversity and our ongoing investment in innovative data integration capabilities. The MQ measures both the strength of the vision as well as ability to execute. The 2026 iteration firmly places Microsoft as a leader. We agree with Gartner’s perspective that our success hinges on delivering seamless integration across Microsoft’s Data Integration portfolio, unifying experiences across data sources, and building a strong, engaged community that drives adoption and advocacy. The report also observed that with a broad global presence serving customers across industries, we continue to invest in advancing Fabric’s data integration capabilities, including real-time data, AI enablement, and data governance, helping organizations unlock greater value from their data. Figure: Magic Quadrant for Data Integration Tools Our key strengths Unified vision for data management: Microsoft Fabric brings together data integration and data management in a unified platform, empowering both technical and business users to build, manage, and deliver end-to-end data pipelines. This includes support for diverse data integration scenarios and AI-driven workloads, simplifying how organizations turn data into value. Open ecosystem and interoperability: We continue to expand Fabric’s interoperability capabilities, making it easier for customers to connect, integrate, and work with data wherever it lives. From expanding Mirroring and OneLake shortcuts to integrating with Apache Spark and Apache Airflow, and partnering with dbt for native transformations, we are committed to providing customers with flexibility and choice. Thriving community and partner ecosystem: Our growing global partner ecosystem and Fabric community are critical to accelerating customer success. Through investments in partner enablement, systems integrator expertise, and global events and conferences, we are expanding access to the skills, resources, and support customers need to realize the full potential of Microsoft’s Data Integration portfolio. In addition, with the breadth and depth of today’s data estate, governance is critical. Capabilities like data lineage, policy enforcements, observability and monitoring give customers the confidence to deploy widely while having the insights they need to monitor, control and optimize. Additionally, the ever-growing range of data sources available with mirroring and shortcuts enable customers to harmonize their multi-cloud and hybrid data estates in OneLake to enable our customers’ frontier transformation ambitions. We believe the entirety of these product truths reflect the priorities our customers have asked for: one platform for every data professional, openness across clouds and formats, deep insights to govern effectively and a thriving ecosystem to help them succeed. Microsoft Fabric: your unified, AI-powered data estate At the core of our data integration strategy is Microsoft Fabric, a unified, AI-powered data and analytics platform designed to simplify the complexities of modern data ecosystems. Now with over 44,000 customers, Fabric delivers an all-in-one, software-as-a-service (SaaS) experience that spans data ingestion, engineering, science, real-time intelligence, and visualization—all built on Microsoft OneLake, a single, unified data lake for your entire organization. With OneLake, you load your data once and use that single copy across every Fabric workload and engine, eliminating duplication and reducing complexity. Built on open standards such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg, OneLake lets Delta tables be accessed as Iceberg without data movement or conversion, while the OneLake catalog provides a central hub for data discovery, governance, and collaboration. Many ways to bring data into OneLake Fabric Data Factory Fabric Data Factory integrates seamlessly with OneLake, offering cloud-scale services for data movement, orchestration, transformation, deployment, and monitoring. With native dbt support and Apache Airflow integration, data teams can use the tools they already know to tackle even the most complex ETL scenarios. Customers with existing SSIS investments can retain those workloads while modernizing with Fabric, and the on-premises data gateway connects Fabric to data behind private networks. Shortcuts and mirroring Shortcuts and mirroring offer a zero-copy, zero-ETL approach to bringing data into OneLake. Shortcuts virtualize data from across clouds—including Amazon S3 and Google Cloud Storage—directly into OneLake, enabling near real-time analysis through live connections to the source. Mirroring replicates operational databases and data warehouses, including Google BigQuery, into the lake, keeping data synchronized and ready for analytics. Partnerships with Snowflake, Databricks, and SAP extend bidirectional data sharing even further. Real-Time Intelligence Fabric Real-Time Intelligence empowers organizations to ingest and process streaming and high-granularity data instantly, driving real-time insights and automated decision-making for scenarios such as IoT analytics, fraud detection, and operational dashboards. Whether through batch processing, incremental updates, or real-time streaming, Fabric gives organizations a secure, scalable foundation for every data integration pattern—across cloud, multicloud, and hybrid environments. Customer success Real customer experiences show how Microsoft Fabric is making a measurable difference. Organizations like IWG, Mercedes Benz, Mediterranean Shipping Company, LSEG, and EY have adopted Microsoft Fabric to build the robust data foundation required for AI. At IWG, shortcuts in OneLake replaced costly pipelines and data movement, helping cut report generation time by 90% and giving 2,000 users access to data insights. "Microsoft Fabric was a game changer because of its ability to create shortcuts without physically moving data from one place to another. Before, if I had to incorporate three sources, I had to create pipelines to bring in the data. That pipeline had a cost. The data movement had a cost. With Fabric, it's two clicks and that's it." — José Viegas, Senior Data Architect, IWG Looking ahead Six years in, the conversation has shifted from bringing data together to putting it to work. This year's recognition we feel reflects that shift: an open platform that meets data wherever it lives, a growing community of partners and experts, and customers like IWG turning faster access to data into real business results. We're grateful to the customers, partners, and Fabric community who help shape what we build. title: Power BI reports support OAP exceptions for semantic models in separate workspaces (Preview)
text: Workspace outbound access protection (OAP) helps you control where data in a Microsoft Fabric workspace can flow. The initial preview for Power BI reports , launched in June, required a report in an OAP-protected workspace to use a semantic model in that same workspace. Customer feedback highlighted that this was too restrictive. With this improvement, a report can now query a semantic model in another workspace provided a workspace administrator explicitly allowed that destination through an OAP exception policy. Apply exception policies to allow report-to-model connections OAP continues to block outbound report-to-model connections by default. When a report opens, Power BI evaluates the report workspace policy before it renders the report in the browser. If the destination workspace is covered by an applicable exception, the report can connect to its semantic model. Otherwise, Power BI blocks the connection, and the report does not open. The report honors the policy that a workspace admin configured for the semantic model destination. You don't configure an exception on each report, and you don't need to move the report and semantic model into the same workspace. The OAP exception policy supports a common Power BI architecture: a central team manages shared semantic models in one workspace, while business teams build reports in separate workspaces. You can preserve that separation of ownership without removing the outbound boundary from the report workspace. See the improvement in action The following example shows a report stored in an OAP-protected workspace, and its semantic model is stored in another workspace. First, the report does not have an applicable exception policy. Power BI blocks the cross-workspace connection and displays the following error because the report can't access its semantic model. Figure: OAP continues to block outbound report-to-model connections by default. Next, a workspace admin creates an exception policy for the semantic model workspace. In the workspace settings under Outbound networking, select Add new cloud connection rule, select Power BI Semantic Model as the Connection Kind, and select the desired semantic model workspace under Workspace exception, as in the following screenshot. Select Add, and then select Save to save the Data Connection rules. Figure: An OAP exception policy to allow report-to-model connections. After the policy takes effect, the same report loads and its visuals render successfully. The report binding doesn't change. The OAP policy determines whether the cross-workspace connection is allowed. The semantic model remains subject to its own OAP controls. Connections from the semantic model to cloud databases, on-premises systems through gateways, lakehouses, warehouses, and other sources are still evaluated against the semantic model workspace's data connection rules . Make sure you enable OAP for both, the report workspace as well as for the semantic model workspace. Next steps Work with your workspace admin to confirm that your report workspace meets the OAP prerequisites and that OAP is enabled. Then create an exception policy for each approved semantic model destination. Policy changes can take about 15 minutes to propagate. For configuration details, refer to the Workspace outbound access protection for Power BI reports documentation. To understand downstream enforcement, refer to Workspace outbound access protection for semantic models .

title: Build more connected workflows with Fabric Actions and Business Actions in Fabric Pipelines (Preview)
text: Modern data workflows rarely stop at moving and transforming data. Once data is ready, you may need to trigger another operation in Fabric, refresh a semantic model, update a business application, send a notification, generate a document, or kick off the next step in a business process. With Fabric Actions and Business Actions activities in Microsoft Fabric Data Factory, you can bring these steps directly into your Fabric pipelines. Together, these activities make it easier to orchestrate workflows across Fabric and the business applications your organization relies on, without having to build and maintain custom API integrations for every scenario. We’re continuing to expand what you can do with these activities, with support for more Fabric operations and 25 additional third-party connectors for Business Actions. Bring Fabric operations directly into your pipelines The Fabric Actions activity lets you invoke supported Fabric REST API operations directly from a pipeline. Instead of manually constructing REST API requests and managing the underlying authentication and request details, you can select the Fabric operation you need, configure its inputs, and incorporate it into the rest of your pipeline workflow. We’re expanding the range of supported Fabric actions across experiences such as Lakehouse, Warehouse, Notebook, Copy Job, Dataflow, Eventhouse, Eventstream, semantic models, OneLake shortcuts, Workspaces, Capacity, and more. This gives you more ways to automate Fabric as part of an end-to-end workflow. For example, you could run a Notebook as part of your data processing flow, manage a OneLake shortcut, perform a Lakehouse operation, or refresh a semantic model after new data is ready, all orchestrated from the same pipeline. Fabric Actions also provides built-in connection and credential handling, helping reduce the authentication and integration work that would otherwise be required when calling supported Fabric APIs directly. The following visual shows how you can select and configure a Fabric operation directly within your pipeline. Figure: Invoke supported Fabric operations directly from your pipeline with Fabric Actions. Connect your pipelines to more business applications While Fabric Actions helps you orchestrate operations within Fabric, Business Actions helps connect your data workflows to the business applications and services where business processes happen. With this release, we’re expanding Business Actions with 25 additional third-party connectors, opening new possibilities across CRM, communications, document generation and signing, security, financial planning, project management, marketing, and more. For example, you can use Business Actions to: Send SMS notifications with D7SMS . Generate contracts, invoices, proposals, and other documents with Formstack Documents . Automate CRM and sales processes with connectors such as Pipeliner CRM and Commercient . Incorporate electronic signature workflows with Nitro Sign Enterprise Verified . Connect pipeline workflows with project and portfolio management systems. Integrate security and threat intelligence operations with services such as RiskIQ. Automate website content publishing with WP Connectr for WordPress . These additions build on the Business Actions experience to give pipeline authors more ways to connect data with the systems and processes that teams use every day. The following visual highlights some of the business applications that can be connected to your pipeline using Business Actions. Figure: Connect your pipelines to business applications and services with Business Actions. Find and configure the action you need As we expand the actions available to pipeline authors, we’re also making them easier to discover and configure. Discover Fabric operations With the updated Fabric Actions experience, you can browse or search for supported Fabric operations instead of needing to know the underlying REST API endpoint ahead of time. Once you select an operation, the activity surfaces the relevant configuration and required parameters. You can then select an existing Fabric connection or create one, provide the required inputs, and use dynamic content where supported. The following visual shows the updated experience for discovering the Fabric operation you want to use. Figure: Browse supported Fabric operations from the Fabric Actions picker. Figure: Search for supported Fabric operations from the Fabric Actions picker. Configure your action Getting started is straightforward. Add Fabric Actions or Business Actions to your pipeline, find the operation you want to perform, configure the required inputs and connection, and incorporate the activity into your pipeline flow. For Fabric Actions: Create or open a pipeline in Microsoft Fabric Data Factory. Add the Fabric Actions activity to the pipeline. Browse or search for the Fabric operation you want to perform. Select or create a Fabric connection. Configure the required inputs. Save and run your pipeline. When the activity runs, the selected Fabric operation executes as part of the pipeline, with its response available through the activity output. Business Actions follows the same principle by providing structured configuration for supported business application operations, so you can incorporate business processes without starting from a custom API integration. Go from data workflows to business workflows The real power comes from combining Fabric Actions and Business Actions with the rest of your pipeline. Consider a pipeline that processes the latest sales data. Once processing completes, the same pipeline could refresh the semantic model used for reporting, create or update a record in a CRM system, generate a customer document, and send a notification that the latest information is ready. Or imagine a document workflow where a pipeline processes business data, generates a contract from that data, starts an electronic signature process, and continues downstream processing once the appropriate business step has taken place. Rather than building separate integrations for each part of the process, you can bring data processing, Fabric operations, and business actions together as part of a larger orchestrated workflow. This allows your pipelines to coordinate not only what happens to your data, but what happens next because of your data. The following visual shows an example of an end-to-end pipeline that brings data processing, Fabric operations, and business processes together. Figure: Bring data, Fabric operations, and business actions together in a single pipeline. More actions, more possibilities We’re continuing to expand both Fabric Actions and Business Actions to give pipeline authors more ways to connect their data workflows with the next step in their business process. For Fabric Actions, that means broader coverage across Fabric workloads and platform operations, from Lakehouse, Warehouse, Notebook, and Copy Job to semantic models, OneLake shortcuts, Workspaces, Capacity, and more. For Business Actions, that means expanding the connector ecosystem so pipelines can interact with more of the applications and services organizations use every day. Our goal is to make these integrations easier to discover, configure, and incorporate into the pipelines you already build, so you can spend less time building integration plumbing and more time building end-to-end workflows. Get started To get started, open a pipeline in Microsoft Fabric Data Factory and explore the Fabric Actions and Business Actions activities. Whether you’re automating an operation within Fabric, connecting your pipeline to a downstream business application, or building a workflow that spans both, Fabric Actions and Business Actions give you more ways to turn data into action directly from Fabric Pipelines. title: Regular expression functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
text: Data warehouses routinely ingest valuable information embedded in free text, where inconsistent structure makes it difficult to query, connect, and analyze. Incoming values can also require quality checks before they reach curated tables. Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint now support scalar regular expression functions in preview, so you can extract useful values, validate formats, standardize text, and mask sensitive data directly in T-SQL instead of adding a separate processing step. What’s new in preview Regular expressions provide a concise way to recognize, extract, and transform complex text patterns that would otherwise require multiple string operations. The preview introduces the following scalar functions: REGEXP_LIKE : checks whether text matches a pattern. REGEXP_REPLACE : replaces matching text to clean, standardize, or mask values. REGEXP_SUBSTR : extracts a substring that matches a pattern. REGEXP_INSTR : returns the position of a matching substring. REGEXP_COUNT : counts pattern occurrences in a string. Use these functions during refinement to turn identifiers embedded in free text into structured values and to flag malformed records before they reach downstream systems. The following scenarios demonstrate both uses. Extract useful values from raw text In this fictional example, inbound customer emails land in bronze.EmailMessages. The Sender column contains a value such as “Avery Smith”, and an order reference such as “ORD-10293” may appear in the Subject column. REGEXP_SUBSTR extracts the sender’s name, email address, company identifier, and order number as structured values that can be related to curated customer, company, and order data. Figure: Extracting structured values from email message text. For “Avery Smith ”, the query returns “Avery Smith” as the Name, “avery@contoso.com” as the Email, and “contoso” as the Company. It also extracts the order number from the Subject column. Validate contact data before it reaches downstream systems Contact data in the silver.DimCustomer table can contain missing characters, extra spaces, or email addresses that do not follow the expected format. REGEXP_LIKE identifies records that fail the format check, so you can review, correct, or quarantine them before the dimension feeds reports, campaigns, and downstream applications. SELECT SourceCustomerId, EmailAddress FROM silver.DimCustomer WHERE NOT REGEXP_LIKE(EmailAddress, '^[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$'); The query isolates email addresses that do not match the expected format so they can be reviewed, corrected, or quarantined before the customer dimension is released to downstream consumers. Conclusion Regular expression functions help turn hard-to-use text into structured, trustworthy warehouse data. You can extract sender, company, and order details from inbound emails and validate contact values during refinement, all with concise T-SQL close to the source. The result is information that is easier to connect, analyze, and trust. Explore the preview and learn how to use regular expression functions in Fabric Data Warehouse in the documentation. Share your scenarios and feedback with the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit .

title: Use OneLake as native storage for Azure Databricks (Generally Available)
text: Organizations increasingly use Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks together so teams can choose the tools that best fit their data engineering, analytics, and AI workloads while working from a common data foundation. OneLake external-location support for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog is now Generally available from the Microsoft Fabric side, with OneLake Security enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. With this integration, supported Unity Catalog-managed data can be stored directly in OneLake. To understand the setup and supported scenarios, Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location . Why this matters Data teams often need Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric in the same architecture. Without a shared storage approach, organizations may create copies of the same data for different platforms, introduce pipelines whose primary purpose is synchronization, and manage access independently across multiple storage locations. Using OneLake as managed storage for supported Unity Catalog objects gives organizations a common physical data foundation while preserving flexibility in the services used above it. Azure Databricks continues to provide compute and Unity Catalog management, while OneLake provides the storage destination and Fabric-side data-access controls. What's new in this release This release builds on the Beta announcement , which introduced OneLake external-location support for Unity Catalog. OneLake Security is now enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items, giving administrators explicit control over which approved identities can discover, read, or write data in OneLake. The updated security experience helps platform teams move from testing connectivity to planning controlled adoption. Administrators can evaluate where Azure Databricks data should be stored and explicitly configure the identities and permissions required to access it. One shared data foundation, with flexibility above it Use OneLake as the storage foundation Azure Databricks workloads can create supported Unity Catalog-managed data directly in OneLake. A Unity Catalog external location points to an Azure Databricks Storage item in OneLake, and a catalog or schema can use that external location as managed storage. Control access explicitly OneLake Security is enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. Administrators can assign discovery, read, or write permissions based on the access each identity requires. Continue using Unity Catalog-managed objects Teams can continue using Azure Databricks and Unity Catalog to create and manage supported managed tables, volumes, views, materialized views, and streaming tables. The objects remain managed through the Azure Databricks experience while their underlying supported data is stored in OneLake. Keep platform responsibilities clear Azure Databricks remains the environment for Databricks compute and Unity Catalog management. Microsoft Fabric provides the capacity-backed workspace and Azure Databricks Storage item, while OneLake provides the physical storage foundation and corresponding Fabric-side access controls. How it works Provision storage in Microsoft Fabric: Create a capacity-backed Fabric workspace and an Azure Databricks Storage item. The storage item provides the OneLake location used by the integration. Configure identity and access: Use an Access Connector for Azure Databricks with a managed identity, or an approved service principal. Grant the identity the required Fabric workspace or item access and configure the applicable OneLake Security permissions. Create the Unity Catalog connection: In Azure Databricks, create a storage credential for the approved identity, and then create a OneLake external location that points to the Azure Databricks Storage item. Create Unity Catalog objects: Configure a catalog or schema to use the OneLake external location as managed storage. Data written by supported Azure Databricks workloads is then stored directly in OneLake. Security and governance A shared data foundation does not create a single permission model. Access must be configured in both Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric so that users and workloads can reach only the objects and data they require. Use a managed identity or service principal approved for the workload. Grant only the required Fabric workspace or item permission. Configure the applicable OneLake Security role with the required discovery, read, or write permissions. Configure Unity Catalog permissions for the corresponding Databricks objects and validate end-to-end access before broader rollout. Keeping these responsibilities separate helps administrators apply least-privilege access on both sides. It also makes troubleshooting clearer because Databricks object permissions and OneLake data permissions can be evaluated independently. Get started Ready to use OneLake as managed storage for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog objects? Start with the Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location tutorial and plan your deployment.

title: Power Query Corner: Finding and connecting to data in the new experience (Preview)
text: About this series This is the first in a six-part Power Query Corner series exploring the new Power Query experience. Each post takes a closer look at a different part of the experience, including what’s changing, why it matters, and how you can put it to work. Getting data doesn't always begin with a connector name. You might know which database to use, recognize a team-maintained Fabric item, want to return to a source from yesterday, or already have the query logic you need. A connector list is useful once you've decided how to connect. But choosing the right data often comes before that decision. We moved to a module-based approach so Get data can support those different starting points, rather than making every task begin with the same connector picker. The idea is simple: start with what you know, then follow the route that fits the task . Modules organize discovery, reconnection, and authoring around that idea. They don't remove the need to authenticate, select the right objects, inspect a preview, or maintain the query afterward. This first Power Query Corner issue follows a sales-report scenario in the new Power BI Desktop experience. It also uses clearly labeled Power Query Online examples to explain the wider design, then looks at the five most frequently reported Get Data problems and the work addressing them. The customer-feedback analysis draws on publicly available reports in our community forum thread , where we track feedback on the new Power Query experience. Choose a Get data route that matches your task Priya is preparing a regional sales review. A colleague offers a spreadsheet export, but the team also maintains sales data in Fabric. Before choosing Excel or another connector, she needs to decide whether to reuse that maintained item, return to a known source, or establish a new connection. A module is a task-focused view inside Get data. Home brings the available routes together; the other modules give each task room for its own search, context, and actions. In Desktop, that includes New, Recent data, OneLake catalog, Blank table, and Blank query. The names and choices offered depend on the product hosting Power Query. Figure: Home brings different starting points into one Get data experience. View more opens the corresponding full module; a source shortcut starts that source's connection flow. Official Desktop documentation screenshot. Source: Microsoft Learn Know the source? Keep the direct route. If Priya already has the required server, file location, or service URL, New remains the straightforward route: search for the connector or browse its category, then supply the required settings. Home can provide a shortcut without first opening the full list. Selecting a connector starts the connection workflow; it doesn't immediately load data. This matters for familiar work. The module-based approach isn't an instruction to browse every module before choosing a CSV file. It should preserve a direct path for someone who already knows the source. Know the business data? Discover the item first. If Priya knows the team maintains sales data but doesn't know its endpoint, OneLake catalog gives her a different starting point. She can find an item by its business context, then review its type, owner, location, and available endorsement or sensitivity information before deciding to connect. Imagine two items, both named Sales: one is in the team's maintained reporting location, while the other belongs to a personal test project. The name alone isn't enough. Catalog context helps Priya ask the right questions before she commits the report to a source. Endorsement is a useful signal, not a guarantee of suitability, and discovering an item does not grant permission to read it. The benefit is not merely another way to open the same dialog: it lets Priya choose an appropriate existing data item before looking up connection details or creating another export. To learn more, refer to the OneLake catalog overview for the catalog's broader discovery, governance, and security roles. Used it before, or need a small starting table? Recent data is the route back to a source Priya already recognizes. It avoids starting the decision again at the connector list, but a recent entry isn't a snapshot of the data or a guarantee that its location and permissions are unchanged. Blank table and Blank query answer a different question: what if the starting point isn't an external source? Priya might enter a small RegionCode-to-RegionName mapping in Blank table or paste a self-contained M expression into Blank query. M is Power Query's formula language. Entered values become part of the query; pasting a spreadsheet's values does not create a refreshable connection to that spreadsheet. Power Query Online examples, not Desktop capabilities The broader module design also accommodates finding a source by browsing the place where it lives. Recognizing an Azure resource or a SharePoint site is different from knowing its server address or file URL. Where those source-browsing experiences are offered, they can carry the user from a recognizable location to the contents they want. Browsing into a location and selecting it for a connection are different actions, and a file's contents are different from a folder's file list. Browse Azure, SharePoint browsing, and Upload is not currently available as modules in Power BI Desktop. They are part of Dataflow Gen2, and some are also available in Power BI web modeling; the available modules vary by host. There is no committed release date for these modules in Power BI Desktop. This module distinction should not be confused with the availability of individual Azure or SharePoint connectors through New. Search scope, filters, previews, and available actions depend on the browser and host. The useful principle is to support recognition and navigation where appropriate while retaining direct connector configuration. Dataflow Gen2 illustrates another distinction: reusing data is not the same as reusing query logic . OneLake catalog helps find a data item; My Queries holds personal M scripts; Shared queries (Preview) let authors import logic shared by others. For example, Priya could reuse an existing region-cleanup script in a dataflow instead of recreating those transformations. Importing shared logic creates an independent copy, not a live link to its original, and does not transfer credentials or destinations. To learn more, refer to the My Queries or Shared Queries documentation. Figure: Dataflow Gen2 example, not Power BI Desktop: My Queries is a personal library of query logic, distinct from recent sources and from the separate Shared queries module. This published Dataflow Gen2 screenshot illustrates why different tasks need different entry points. Source: Microsoft Learn Modules can also support tasks such as describing transformations with Copilot in Dataflow Gen2, subject to that feature's requirements. That does not make every Power Query Online module a Desktop capability. Use Get Data in Dataflow Gen2 for its supported entry points and Data sources in Power BI Desktop for Desktop. Try it: Choose and preview a sales source in Power BI Desktop or web modeling You can use the October 2026 release of Power BI Desktop or try Power BI web modeling today with an authorized source in a nonproduction report. In Desktop, enable the preview: navigate to File > Options and settings > Options > Preview features, select New Power Query experience, and select OK.
